body.objective: Students will be able to analyze a monologue for subtext.
body.iCan: I can analyze a monologue for subtext.
successCriteria: I can identify subtext in a monologue
I can find the character's intention for each section
I can mark a script to show subtext and intention
body.hook: When someone says "No, really, I'm happy for you" through clenched teeth, the words say one thing and the meaning says another. That hidden meaning is subtext, and finding it is how actors make monologues come alive.

vocabulary.definition: A long speech by one character.
The meaning beneath the words; what the character really thinks or feels.
What the character is trying to do to the listener with their words.
Studying a script closely to understand character and meaning.
The facts of the situation: who, where, when and what just happened.
A section of a monologue with one intention.

study.title: Under the Words
study.question: How do actors find the meaning beneath the words?
study.passage:
Monologue (written for this lesson):
SAM (age 15, speaking to an older sister who is leaving for university):
"So you're actually going. Great. That's great. No, I mean it. You'll have your own room, your own friends, no little brother borrowing your chargers. You won't miss the pancakes on Saturdays, I bet. They probably have better pancakes there. Anyway, I made you something. It's stupid. It's just a playlist. All the songs from the car rides to Grandma's. You don't have to listen to it. You'll probably be too busy. Just... call sometimes, okay? Not every day. That'd be weird. Just sometimes."
Task: 1. Given circumstances: Who is Sam talking to? Where? What just happened? 2. Divide the monologue into units where the intention changes. 3. For each line, write the subtext in brackets: "Great. That's great." [I don't want you to go.] 4. Give each unit an intention verb: to pretend, to tease, to hide, to give, to ask.
study.source: Original monologue written for this lesson.
steps: Write the subtext for each line
Give each unit an intention verb
discussion: Which line comes closest to saying the truth?
How would knowing the subtext change your delivery?
study.product: Submit a marked script of the monologue showing units, subtext for every line and an intention verb for each unit.

body.objective: Students will be able to use pace and pause.
body.iCan: I can use pace and pause.
successCriteria: I can vary pace to match a character's thoughts
I can use pauses for meaning
I can use emphasis to highlight key words
body.hook: Two actors can say the same monologue word for word, and one will move you to tears while the other bores you. Often the difference is not the words but the timing: where they speed up, slow down and stop.

vocabulary.definition: How fast or slow a character speaks.
Stressing a word to show its importance.
The pattern of speech, including speed, pauses and stress.
A moment where a new thought begins, often marked by a pause or shift in pace.

study.title: Timing Is Meaning
study.question: How do pace, pause and emphasis shape a monologue?
study.passage:
Activities (written for this lesson), using Sam's monologue:
1. Pace experiment (10 minutes): Say the first unit very fast, then very slow. Which suits "pretending to be fine"? Many actors speed up when a character is covering feelings and slow down when the truth comes out.
2. Pause map (10 minutes): Mark pauses with /, longer pauses with //. Where does Sam need a breath to find courage? Where does he stop himself? Example: "Just... // call sometimes, okay? / Not every day."
3. Emphasis (10 minutes): Underline one key word per sentence. Try different words: "You won't miss the pancakes" versus "You won't miss the pancakes" versus "You won't miss the pancakes."
4. Combine (15 minutes): In pairs, rehearse the monologue using your pace, pause and emphasis choices. The partner plays the silent sister, reacting honestly. Then swap.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Experiment with fast and slow pace
Combine choices and rehearse with a silent partner
discussion: Where did you speed up and why?
How did changing emphasis change meaning?
How did your partner's silent reactions affect you?

body.objective: Students will be able to perform a monologue.
successCriteria: I can perform a monologue from memory
I can use focus to show who I'm speaking to
I can reflect on my performance using feedback
body.hook: Standing alone on stage with no scene partner to lean on is one of the bravest things an actor does. A monologue performance puts everything together: subtext, intention, voice, timing and focus.

vocabulary.definition: To learn lines so you can say them without the script.
The person the character speaks to, placed in the space by the actor.
A short introduction before an audition or performance: your name and the piece.

Judging your own performance against criteria.

study.title: Solo Performance
study.question: How do I bring a monologue to life on my own?
study.passage:
Performance guide (written for this lesson):
Choose: Sam's monologue, or an approved monologue from a play (your teacher has a list of age-appropriate public-domain and published pieces, under 2 minutes).
Memorize: learn it unit by unit; record yourself and listen; write the first letter of each word and recite from those.
Imaginary listener: Place your listener just above the audience's heads or slightly to one side, never directly in the front row. Keep them in the same place.
Structure: slate ("My name is ___, and I'll be performing ___"), neutral start, take a breath into character, perform, hold the final moment, return to neutral and say "Thank you."
Criteria (self and peer): voice (projection, clarity), subtext and intention, pace and pause, focus and physicality, commitment.
After performing, write a self-assessment, then compare with peer feedback.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Practise the slate and neutral start
Self-assess and compare with peer feedback
discussion: Where did you place your listener and why?
Which unit did you perform best?
What happened when you felt nervous?
How did peer feedback compare with your self-assessment?
study.product: Perform your monologue with a slate and complete a self-assessment against the five criteria.
